title: India, 1930
tagline: The Salt March, a Nobel Prize for Raman and the Deccan Queen.

morningRoutine.detail: Common rice sold retail at about Rs 7.4 a maund in Bombay and Rs 10 in Delhi in 1930, as prices fell in the depression.

source.label: Statistical Abstract relating to British India, 1923-24 to 1932-33 (Government of India, 1935), tables 298 and 300, pp. 774 and 778, via the Internet Archive

morningRoutine.detail: After the private Indian Broadcasting Company went into liquidation on 1 March 1930, the government took over its stations and started the Indian State Broadcasting Service.
The Deccan Queen began running between Bombay and Poona on 1 June 1930, described as India's first superfast, electric-hauled long-distance train.
Gandhi's English weekly Young India was in its twelfth year; it ran from 1919 to 1931.

technology.name: The Deccan Queen
technology.description: The Deccan Queen began running on 1 June 1930 between Bombay and Poona. It is described as India's first superfast, long-distance electric-hauled and vestibuled train, with a women-only car and a dining car.

technology.name: State broadcasting begins
technology.description: After the private Indian Broadcasting Company went into liquidation on 1 March 1930, the government took over its stations and launched the Indian State Broadcasting Service on 1 April 1930.

technology.name: The Raman effect
technology.description: C. V. Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for his work on the scattering of light and for the discovery of the effect named after him'.

source.label: NobelPrize.org: C. V. Raman, facts (The Nobel Prize in Physics 1930)

technology.name: Chandrasekhar's voyage calculations
technology.description: On a trip from India to England in 1930, the young physicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar worked on the statistics of a degenerate Fermi gas, the start of papers that led to the Chandrasekhar limit for white dwarfs.

technology.name: Cinema: Hamara Hindustan
technology.description: A social film directed by R. S. Choudhary for the Imperial Film Company, with Sulochana (Ruby Myers).
